verses.text: After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to see the tomb.
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, for an angel of the Lord descended from heaven, rolled away the stone, and sat on it.
His appearance was like lightning, and his clothes were white as snow.
The guards trembled in fear of him and became like dead men.
But the angel said to the women, "Do not be afraid, for I know that you are looking for Jesus, who was crucified.
He is not here; He has risen, just as He said! Come, see the place where He lay.
Then go quickly and tell His disciples, 'He has risen from the dead and is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see Him.' See, I have told you."
So they hurried away from the tomb in fear and great joy, and ran to tell His disciples.
Suddenly Jesus met them and said, "Greetings!" They came to Him, grasped His feet, and worshiped Him.
"Do not be afraid," said Jesus. "Go and tell My brothers to go to Galilee. There they will see Me."
While the women were on their way, some of the guards went into the city and reported to the chief priests all that had happened.
And after the chief priests had met with the elders and formed a plan, they gave the soldiers a large sum of money
and instructed them: "You are to say, 'His disciples came by night and stole Him away while we were asleep.'
If this report reaches the governor, we will satisfy him and keep you out of trouble."
So the guards took the money and did as they were instructed. And this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day.
Meanwhile, the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated.
When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted.
Then Jesus came to them and said, "All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.
Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age."

context.author: Matthew, writing to a Jewish audience
context.genre: Narrative closing with direct commissioning speech — the empty tomb, the risen Jesus meeting the women, the authorities' cover-up attempt, and the Great Commission that ends the Gospel.
context.audience: Jewish-Christian readers, given the climactic resolution to everything the Gospel has pointed toward since chapter 16's first passion prediction — and sent outward, in the closing verses, toward the whole world.
context.mapLabel: THE TOMB, JERUSALEM → A MOUNTAIN IN GALILEE
context.setting: Dawn on the first day of the week — Sunday, following the Sabbath rest. Roman guard units assigned to a tomb typically numbered four to sixteen soldiers; falling asleep on duty carried the death penalty, which explains why they needed a substantial bribe to accept blame for an empty tomb.
context.custom: Women preparing to visit and anoint a body (implied here, explicit in the other Gospels) reflects standard first-century burial custom — visiting a tomb on the third day was also common practice, intended to confirm death had truly occurred.
context.timelineImmediate: This is the Gospel's climax and closing scene — the empty tomb resolves everything Jesus predicted about His own death and resurrection, and the Great Commission on the Galilean mountain closes the book by sending the story forward into the disciples' — and the reader's — own future.
context.timelineBible: Jesus' resurrection ministry deliberately returns to Galilee (v.7, 16) — the same region where His public ministry first began in chapter 4 — framing the whole Gospel as a journey that starts and ends in the same place, now sending outward to "all nations" rather than staying local.

translation.meaning: A passive verb form — implying God's own action in raising Jesus, rather than Jesus raising Himself under His own power alone.

occurrences.note: A very common word overall (also used for ordinary waking or healing) — its meaning here comes entirely from context, not rarity.

translation.meaning: Not merely "convert" but form into committed, lifelong learners and followers — a deeper, ongoing relationship than a single decision.

occurrences.note: Used only four times in the whole New Testament — and three of those four are in Matthew alone.

translation.meaning: Complete, comprehensive authority — echoing Daniel 7:14's vision of the Son of Man receiving dominion, glory, and a kingdom from God directly.

translation.english: to the end of the age
translation.greek: ἕως τῆς συντελείας τοῦ αἰῶνος (heōs tēs synteleias tou aiōnos)
translation.meaning: Until the completion of the present world order — Jesus' promised presence isn't temporary but spans the entire era of the Gospel's proclamation.

gospelParallels.note: Mark's account of the empty tomb, ending abruptly with the women's fear and amazement.
Luke's version, which adds the road to Emmaus and a Jerusalem appearance.
John's fuller account, including Thomas's doubt and a breakfast appearance by the Sea of Galilee.

otBackground.note: The Son of Man receiving all authority, glory, and an everlasting kingdom — directly echoed in Jesus' declaration in v.18.
God's promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring — finding its fulfillment in the Great Commission's reach to "all nations."
"You will not abandon my soul to Sheol" — read by the early church as a resurrection prophecy fulfilled in this chapter.

context.sparkNotes: Women find the tomb empty, and Jesus commissions His eleven disciples in Galilee to make disciples of all nations. "Make disciples" appears only four times in the whole New Testament, three of them in Matthew alone — and Jesus' claim to "all authority" directly echoes Daniel 7:13-14's vision of dominion given to the Son of Man.

commentary.note: Henry sees deliberate design in a small detail people often skip past: God ordered it so that witnesses would see Christ risen, but not actually see him rise — the same principle, he notes, that governed the incarnation itself, "a mystery... so was this second incarnation." He also poetically contrasts the earth's two reactions: it "shook for fear" receiving Christ's body at death, then "leaped for joy" at His exaltation in the resurrection earthquake.

On the soldiers' bribed cover story, Henry notes it had remarkable staying power — citing Justin Martyr's record that the Jewish authorities were still circulating this same fabricated "stolen body" explanation to Jewish communities abroad decades later, treating it as a deliberate, sustained campaign rather than a one-time lie.

Gill makes a careful grammatical point about 'teach all nations, baptizing them': in the Greek, 'them' doesn't grammatically match 'all nations' (a neuter noun) but rather 'disciples,' implied by the verb 'make disciples' just before it — meaning the command is to baptize those actually taught and won as disciples, not indiscriminately baptize entire populations.
